a: Citizens can become co-owners of wind farms
Wind turbines stand only in uninhabited areas
Wind turbines are switched off at night
61274.e: At the Middelgrunden wind farm off Copenhagen, half of the 20 turbines belong to a cooperative with thousands of members. Such citizen participation has strengthened acceptance of wind power in Denmark.
61274.m: In Denmark many citizens have a stake in wind farms.

61275.q: Which technology does the Gemasolar solar power station near Seville use?
a: Solar tower with molten salt storage
61275.e: Thousands of mirrors focus sunlight onto a tower in which molten salt is heated. The heat store allows electricity to be produced at night as well.
61275.m: Thanks to its salt store, Gemasolar can also supply electricity at night.

61276.q: Which power station near Seville was Europe's first commercial solar tower power station in 2007?
61276.e: PS10 near Sanlúcar la Mayor was connected to the grid in 2007 and uses 624 mirrors that direct the light onto a tower. Gemasolar followed in 2011.
61276.m: PS10 near Seville was Europe's first commercial solar tower power station.

61277.q: What is the Plataforma Solar de Almería?
a: A large research centre for concentrated solar technology
The largest solar park in Europe
A port for importing solar cells
A factory for solar roof tiles
61277.e: The Plataforma Solar de Almería in Andalusia is Europe's largest research centre for solar thermal energy. Mirror power stations and storage systems are tested there.
61277.m: Concentrated solar technology is researched in Almería.

61278.q: Which technology do the Andasol power stations in the province of Granada use?
61278.e: Andasol uses long parabolic trough mirrors that heat a thermal oil. A salt store allows several hours of operation without sunshine.
61278.m: Andasol works with parabolic troughs and a salt store.

61279.q: Why is southern Spain especially well suited to solar energy?
a: Strong sunshine and many hours of sun
Lots of snow to reflect light
61279.e: With about 3,000 hours of sunshine a year, Andalusia and Extremadura are among the sunniest regions in Europe. There are also large, thinly populated areas.
61279.m: Southern Spain offers lots of sun and lots of space for solar plants.

61280.q: Which controversial charge on self-consumed solar power did Spain abolish in 2018?
a: The grid fee for wind farms
61280.e: A decree of 2015 placed charges on solar power used by the producers themselves, which was criticised as an “impuesto al sol” (sun tax). It was repealed in 2018, after which solar expansion picked up sharply.
61280.m: After the sun tax ended in 2018, solar energy boomed in Spain.

61281.q: In which Spanish region are large photovoltaic parks such as Núñez de Balboa and Francisco Pizarro?
61281.e: Both parks are in Extremadura, which borders Portugal, and with hundreds of megawatts they are among the largest solar parks in Europe.
61281.m: Extremadura is a stronghold of Spanish solar parks.

61282.q: What happened on the Iberian Peninsula on 28 April 2025 that fuelled the debate about grid stability with lots of solar power?
a: A record hailstorm on solar parks
The shutdown of all nuclear power stations
61282.e: On 28 April 2025 the power went off almost everywhere in Spain and Portugal for hours. Afterwards there was intense debate about how grids with a high share of solar power can stay stable.
61282.m: The 2025 blackout showed how important stable grids are.

61283.q: Roughly what share of Norway's electricity comes from hydropower?
61283.e: Norway generates about 90 per cent of its electricity from hydropower, making it the largest hydropower producer in Europe. By comparison, in Switzerland it is about 60 per cent.
61283.m: Norway gets almost all its electricity from hydropower.

61284.q: Which state-owned company is Norway's largest hydropower producer?
61284.e: Statkraft is wholly owned by the state and is considered the largest producer of renewable energy in Europe. It runs hundreds of hydropower stations.
61284.m: Statkraft is Norway's state hydropower company.

61285.q: Which undersea cable has connected Norway directly with Germany since 2021?
61285.e: NordLink is a direct current cable about 620 kilometres long between southern Norway and Schleswig-Holstein. It exchanges Norwegian hydropower for German wind power.
61285.m: NordLink connects Norwegian hydropower with Germany.

61286.q: Why is Norway often called the “battery of Europe”?
a: Its reservoirs can store energy and release it flexibly
It produces the most lithium batteries
It stores Europe's natural gas reserves
It has the largest coal stocks
61286.e: The large reservoirs hold about half of Europe's storage capacity. Water can be held back when wind and sun are producing a lot, and used to generate electricity when needed.
61286.m: Norway's reservoirs work like a giant battery.

61287.q: Which company was founded in 1905 to use hydropower to make artificial fertiliser?
61287.e: Norsk Hydro used the waterfalls near Rjukan and Notodden to make nitrogen fertiliser. Hydropower made Norway an industrial location early on.
61287.m: Norsk Hydro began in 1905 using hydropower for fertiliser.

61288.q: Why is Norway so well suited to hydropower?
a: Lots of rain and snow and big height differences down to the sea
Lakes that are frozen all year
61288.e: A lot of rain and snow falls on the mountains from the Atlantic. The water rushes down over big height differences to the coast, and hundreds of power stations use this energy.
61288.m: Rain and mountains make Norway a hydropower country.

61289.q: Which undersea cable has connected Norway with Great Britain since 2021 and was the longest undersea power cable in the world when it opened?
61289.e: North Sea Link runs about 720 kilometres from Kvilldal to Blyth in England. It allows electricity to be exchanged in both directions.
61289.m: North Sea Link connects Norway and Great Britain.

61290.q: What effect do dry years with little rain have on Norway's electricity market?
61290.e: When the reservoirs are low, there is not enough water to generate electricity. Prices then rise, as in southern Norway in 2022, and the country imports more electricity.
61290.m: In Norway, electricity prices depend heavily on the rain.

61291.q: Which undersea cable, opened in 2008, connects Norway with the Netherlands?
61291.e: NorNed is about 580 kilometres long and was the longest undersea power cable in the world when it opened. It allows electricity trading between the two countries.
61291.m: Since 2008 NorNed has connected Norway with the Netherlands.

61292.q: When did the Chernobyl nuclear disaster happen?
61292.e: In the night of 26 April 1986, Unit 4 of the Chernobyl nuclear power station exploded. It was the worst accident in the history of civil nuclear power.

61293.q: What did the Chernobyl reactor lack compared with most Western nuclear power stations?
a: A strong protective shell of steel and concrete
A connection to the power grid
61293.e: The Soviet RBMK reactor type had no full containment. That is why, after the explosion, large amounts of radioactive material escaped into the air unhindered.
61293.m: Chernobyl lacked a strong protective shell around the reactor.

61294.q: What was being carried out in Reactor 4 at Chernobyl on the night of the accident?
61294.e: The aim was to test whether the turbines, as they ran down, would supply enough power for the cooling pumps. Operating errors and design faults led to the explosion.
61294.m: A failed safety test triggered the disaster.

61295.q: Which town near the power station was completely evacuated a day after the accident?
61295.e: Pripyat, the town of the power station workers with about 49,000 inhabitants, was evacuated on 27 April 1986. It is still a ghost town today.
61295.m: After Chernobyl, Pripyat became a ghost town.

61296.q: In which country was the increased radioactivity after Chernobyl first noticed in the West?
61296.e: On 28 April 1986, measuring instruments at the Swedish nuclear power station of Forsmark raised the alarm. This is how the world learned of the accident, which the Soviet Union at first kept quiet.
61296.m: Sweden was the first Western country to detect the radiation from Chernobyl.

61297.q: Which part of Switzerland was most affected by radioactive fallout from Chernobyl?
61297.e: Heavy rain in early May 1986 washed radioactive particles out of the air over Ticino. Fishing bans were imposed there, for example on Lake Lugano.
61297.m: Ticino received the most Chernobyl fallout in Switzerland.

61298.q: What is the protective shell called that was slid over the damaged reactor in 2016?
61298.e: The huge arch structure was built next to the reactor and slid over it in November 2016. It replaces the crumbling sarcophagus of 1986 and is meant to last about 100 years.
61298.m: Since 2016 the New Safe Confinement has covered the damaged reactor.

61299.q: What is the half-life of caesium-137, which made up a large part of the long-term contamination after Chernobyl?
61299.e: Caesium-137 decays with a half-life of about 30 years. That is why wild boar and mushrooms in some areas are still contaminated today. About 8 days is the half-life of iodine-131.
61299.m: Caesium-137 has a half-life of about 30 years.

61300.q: What was the radius of the original exclusion zone around the Chernobyl nuclear power station?
61300.e: After the accident, an exclusion zone with a radius of about 30 kilometres was set up. Over 100,000 people had to leave their homes.
61300.m: There is an exclusion zone of about 30 kilometres around Chernobyl.

61301.q: At which level of the International Nuclear Event Scale (INES) is Chernobyl rated?
61301.e: Chernobyl received the highest INES level, 7, a “major accident”. Only Fukushima in 2011 was rated the same.
61301.m: With INES level 7, Chernobyl counts as a major accident.

61302.q: In which country is the iron ore town of Kiruna?
61302.e: Kiruna lies in Lapland in the far north of Sweden, north of the Arctic Circle. It is the country's northernmost town.
61302.m: Kiruna is in northern Sweden, north of the Arctic Circle.

61303.q: Who owns LKAB, the company that runs the huge iron ore mine in Kiruna?
61303.e: Luossavaara-Kiirunavaara Aktiebolag (LKAB) is wholly owned by the Swedish state. The mine in the Kiirunavaara mountain is the largest underground iron ore mine in the world.
61303.m: Through LKAB, the Kiruna mine belongs to the Swedish state.

61304.q: Through which ice-free port is a large part of Kiruna's ore exported?
61304.e: Since 1902 the Ore Railway has linked Kiruna with Narvik in Norway. Thanks to the Gulf Stream, the port is ice-free all year, while Luleå freezes in winter.
61304.m: Kiruna ore goes out to the world through ice-free Narvik.

61305.q: Why is Kiruna's town centre being moved to a new location?
a: Mining is causing the ground to sink
A glacier is threatening the town
The permafrost is thawing too much
A dam is to be built
61305.e: Mining under the town causes ground movements and cracks. That is why the centre is being moved about 3 kilometres to the east; the new centre opened in 2022.
61305.m: Kiruna is moving because mining is making the ground sink.

61306.q: What is the ore from Kiruna mainly used for?
61306.e: Kiruna mainly mines magnetite, an iron oxide. It is processed into pellets and delivered to steelworks.
61306.m: Iron ore from Kiruna is made into steel.

61307.q: What did LKAB announce for the Kiruna region in January 2023?
a: The largest known deposit of rare earths in Europe
The closure of the mine by 2025
The building of a nuclear power station
61307.e: LKAB reported the largest known deposit of rare earth elements in Europe. These metals are needed, for example, for electric motors and wind turbines.
61307.m: Europe's largest known deposit of rare earths lies near Kiruna.

61308.q: Why is mining in Kiruna no longer done in an open pit but underground?
a: The ore body reaches steeply down to great depths
Open-pit mining is banned in the polar winter
The ore at the surface was radioactive
The open pit lay under a lake
61308.e: Mining began in an open pit in 1898. Because the ore body runs steeply downwards, an open pit would have become wider and more expensive all the time. Today the main level is about 1,365 metres deep.
61308.m: In Kiruna, mining follows the ore far down into the depths.

61309.q: Why was iron ore from Kiruna strategically important in the Second World War?
a: It was an important raw material for German arms production
It was needed for atomic bombs
It was used as fuel for ships
It was Europe's only source of gold
61309.e: Germany got a large part of its iron ore from northern Sweden, partly through Narvik. The battle for Narvik in 1940 was also linked to these ore supplies.
61309.m: Kiruna ore was important for Germany's arms production in the Second World War.

61310.q: Which Swedish project aims to use ore from Kiruna to make steel with hydrogen instead of coal?
61310.e: HYBRIT is a project of SSAB, LKAB and Vattenfall. Instead of coke, hydrogen is used to reduce the iron ore, which produces almost no CO2.
61310.m: HYBRIT aims to make fossil-free steel with hydrogen.

61311.q: What is the decentralised data exchange platform called through which authorities and companies in Estonia have exchanged data securely since 2001?
61311.e: X-Road (X-tee in Estonian) connects the databases of authorities and companies without storing all the data centrally. It is considered the technical backbone of Estonian e-government.
61311.m: In Estonia, X-Road connects the state's databases.

61312.q: Which service did Estonia introduce at the end of 2014 that allows foreigners to get a digital identity from the country?
61312.e: With e-Residency, people from all over the world receive an Estonian digital identity, for example to set up and run a company in the EU online. It is neither citizenship nor a right of residence.
61312.m: E-Residency gives foreigners an Estonian digital identity.

61313.q: What has Estonia been known for worldwide since the local elections of 2005?
a: Legally binding voting over the internet
61313.e: In 2005 Estonia was the first country to hold legally binding internet elections nationwide; since 2007 this has also applied to parliamentary elections. Voters identify themselves with the electronic ID card.
61313.m: Since 2005 Estonia has allowed voting over the internet nationwide.

61314.q: Which well-known internet telephone service was developed largely by Estonian programmers in 2003?
61314.e: Skype's software was programmed by the Estonians Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn. Its success is seen as the starting signal for the Estonian start-up scene.
61314.m: Skype was developed by Estonian programmers.

61315.q: Which event in 2007 brought down the websites of Estonian banks, media and authorities?
a: A fire in the central data centre
61315.e: After the dispute over moving the Soviet Bronze Soldier in Tallinn, Estonia was hit by massive overload attacks (DDoS) in April and May 2007. The case is considered one of the first cyber attacks on an entire state.
61315.m: In 2007 Estonia was the target of massive cyber attacks.

61316.q: Which NATO institution was founded in Tallinn in 2008?
a: A centre of excellence for cyber defence
61316.e: The Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) in Tallinn researches questions of cyber security and international law in cyberspace. It was set up partly in response to Estonia's experience of cyber attacks.
61316.m: NATO's cyber defence centre is in Tallinn.

61317.q: What was the aim of the Estonian schools programme “Tiger Leap” from 1996?
a: To equip all schools with computers and the internet
61317.e: From 1996 the Tiigrihüpe (“Tiger Leap”) programme brought computers and the internet to all Estonian schools. It is seen as an early basis for the population's high digital skills.
61317.m: In the 1990s, Tiger Leap brought the internet to Estonia's schools.

61318.q: What is the Estonian “data embassy” in Luxembourg?
a: A protected server site with backup copies of state data
An embassy that can only be contacted by email
An archive for old paper files
61318.e: In 2017 Estonia and Luxembourg agreed on the world's first data embassy, a server site with diplomatic protection. This keeps important state data available even if Estonia itself is attacked.
61318.m: Estonia's data embassy is in Luxembourg.

61319.q: What does the “once-only principle” used in Estonia mean?
a: The state may only ask citizens for data once
Everyone may only vote online once
Every authority has only one website
Passwords may only be used once
61319.e: Under the once-only principle, a person only has to give the state the same information once. Other authorities then get it themselves through the secure data exchange.
61319.m: Under the once-only principle, you only have to give the state the same data once.

61320.q: Which landscape in the Gauja valley around Sigulda is also called “Livonian Switzerland” because of its hills and sandstone cliffs?
61320.e: Gauja National Park, founded in 1973, is Latvia's oldest national park. The deeply cut river valley with castles and caves reminded travellers of Switzerland.
61320.m: The area around Sigulda is also called Livonian Switzerland.

61321.q: Which medieval league of towns did Riga belong to as an important trading city?
61321.e: Riga was founded in 1201 and later joined the Hanseatic League. Via the River Daugava, the city traded in timber, furs and grain from the hinterland.

61322.q: For which architecture is the centre of Riga especially famous?
61322.e: Riga has one of the largest collections of Art Nouveau buildings in the world; a large part of the buildings in the centre date from around 1900. Many were designed by the architect Mikhail Eisenstein.
61322.m: Riga is famous for its many Art Nouveau buildings.

61323.q: Which spa town with a sandy beach over 30 kilometres long lies west of Riga on the Gulf of Riga?
61323.e: Jūrmala is made up of a row of former fishing villages and seaside resorts on a narrow strip of land. It is known for its wooden villas and spas.
61323.m: Jūrmala is Latvia's best-known seaside resort.

61324.q: In which year did Latvia introduce the euro?
61324.e: Latvia replaced the lats with the euro on 1 January 2014. The country had already joined the EU in 2004.
61324.m: Latvia has paid with the euro since 2014.

61325.q: What is the historic region in the west of Latvia on the Baltic coast called?
61325.e: Courland (Kurzeme in Latvian) covers western Latvia, with ports such as Liepāja and Ventspils. Latgale lies in the east, Livonia in the north-east and Semigallia in the south.
61325.m: Courland is Latvia's western coastal region.

61326.q: With which of these countries does Latvia not share a land border?
61326.e: Latvia borders Estonia, Russia, Belarus and Lithuania. Poland is separated from Latvia by Lithuania.

61327.q: What was the human chain called that stretched from Tallinn via Riga to Vilnius on 23 August 1989?
61327.e: About two million people formed a chain over 600 kilometres long to remember the Hitler-Stalin Pact of 1939 and to demand independence. The Baltic Way is part of UNESCO's Memory of the World register.
61327.m: In 1989 the Baltic Way linked the three Baltic capitals.

61328.q: Which tradition of the Baltic states is part of UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage and plays a big role in Latvia?
a: The great song and dance festivals
61328.e: The song and dance festivals with tens of thousands of participants take place in Latvia about every five years. They also strengthened national identity during the Soviet era.
61328.m: The song and dance festivals are a shared cultural heritage of the Baltic states.

61329.q: Which island castle from the 14th and 15th centuries stands on an island in Lake Galvė west of Vilnius?
61329.e: Trakai Island Castle was a residence of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania. It was rebuilt from ruins in the 20th century.
61329.m: Trakai Island Castle was the seat of the Lithuanian Grand Dukes.

61330.q: Why was Kaunas the temporary capital of Lithuania between the two World Wars?
a: Because Vilnius had been destroyed in the war
Because Kaunas is by the sea
Because the king lived in Kaunas
61330.e: Poland occupied Vilnius in 1920 and kept the city until 1939. During this time hundreds of modern buildings were built in Kaunas, which have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.
61330.m: Kaunas was the capital while Vilnius belonged to Poland.

61331.q: In which year did Lithuania declare its independence as the first Soviet republic to do so?
61331.e: On 11 March 1990 the Supreme Soviet of Lithuania declared the restoration of independence. The Soviet Union only recognised it in September 1991.
61331.m: In 1990 Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence.

61332.q: What is the Hill of Crosses in Lithuania known for?
a: Tens of thousands of crosses as a sign of resistance
A monastery with the largest bell in Europe
A First World War military cemetery
61332.e: On the hill near Šiauliai, pilgrims have put up tens of thousands of crosses over the decades. The Soviet authorities had it flattened several times, but people kept putting up new crosses.
61332.m: The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai is a symbol of Lithuanian resistance.

61333.q: Which union joined Lithuania and Poland into a single state from 1569?
61333.e: The Union of Lublin in 1569 created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth with a shared king and parliament. It lasted until the partitions of Poland at the end of the 18th century.
61333.m: In 1569 the Union of Lublin created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

61334.q: Which special feature do linguists attribute to the Lithuanian language?
a: It is considered a particularly archaic Indo-European language
It is closely related to Hungarian
It is written in Cyrillic letters
61334.e: Lithuanian has kept many old forms, for example a rich system of cases, and is therefore important for research into the Indo-European parent language. It is written in the Latin alphabet.
61334.m: Lithuanian is considered one of the most archaic living Indo-European languages.

61335.q: According to calculations by the French National Geographic Institute in 1989, where is the geographical centre of Europe?
61335.e: In 1989 the Institut Géographique National calculated the centre of Europe to be near the village of Purnuškės, about 26 kilometres north of Vilnius. Other calculations reach other places depending on the method.
61335.m: A well-known centre of Europe lies north of Vilnius.

61336.q: Why did Lithuania have to close the Ignalina nuclear power station in order to join the EU?
a: Its reactors were like those at Chernobyl
It lay right on the border with Poland
The EU bans all nuclear power stations
61336.e: Ignalina had two reactors of the RBMK type, like those at Chernobyl, and was considered unsafe. The last unit was shut down on 31 December 2009.
61336.m: The Ignalina nuclear power station was closed in 2009.

61337.q: Which river is the longest in Lithuania and flows into the Curonian Lagoon?
61337.e: The Neman (Nemunas in Lithuanian) rises in Belarus and, after about 900 kilometres, flows through a delta into the Curonian Lagoon. Part of its lower course forms the border with Russia.
61337.m: The Neman is Lithuania's longest river.

61338.q: Which river is the longest in Poland and flows into the Baltic Sea near Gdańsk?
61338.e: The Vistula is about 1,050 kilometres long and flows through Kraków and Warsaw, among other cities. Its catchment area covers over half of Poland.
61338.m: The Vistula is Poland's longest river.

61339.q: At 2,499 m, which mountain is the highest peak in Poland?
61339.e: Rysy lies in the High Tatras on the border with Slovakia. Its highest summit is on the Slovak side; the Polish secondary summit is 2,499 m high.
61339.m: Rysy in the High Tatras is Poland's highest mountain.

61340.q: What is Poland's western border, fixed after the Second World War, called?
61340.e: The Oder-Neisse line was set as a provisional border in the Potsdam Agreement of 1945. Reunified Germany recognised it finally in 1990.
61340.m: The Oder-Neisse line forms the border between Poland and Germany.

61341.q: Which region in southern Poland around Katowice is shaped by hard coal mining and heavy industry?
61341.e: The Upper Silesian Industrial Region is one of the largest urban areas in Central Europe. Hard coal mining has shaped the region since the 19th century.
61341.m: Upper Silesia is Poland's coal region.

61342.q: Which mine near Kraków was among the very first UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1978?
61342.e: Salt was mined at Wieliczka from the 13th century until 1996. Its chapels and sculptures carved out of salt are famous.
61342.m: The Wieliczka Salt Mine is one of UNESCO's oldest World Heritage Sites.

61343.q: Which landscape in north-east Poland is known for its thousands of Ice Age lakes?
61343.e: The Masurian Lake District was formed by glaciers of the last Ice Age. Śniardwy is Poland's largest lake.
61343.m: The Masurian Lake District is an Ice Age lake landscape.

61344.q: Which currency does Poland use (as of 2025)?
61344.e: Although Poland has been an EU member since 2004, it has not yet introduced the euro. The złoty is divided into 100 groszy.
61344.m: In Poland you pay with the złoty.

61345.q: Which energy source still provided the largest share of electricity generation in Poland in 2024?
61345.e: Poland still generates more than half of its electricity from hard coal and lignite, more than any other EU country. Wind and solar power, however, are growing strongly.
61345.m: Most of Poland's electricity still comes from coal.

61346.q: What is Słowiński National Park near Łeba on the Baltic coast known for?
61346.e: The shifting dunes near Łeba are up to about 40 metres high and move several metres inland every year. As they do, they bury forest beneath them.
61346.m: In Słowiński National Park, large sand dunes are on the move.

61347.q: Roughly how many inhabitants does Poland have (as of 2024)?
61347.e: At the end of 2024 Poland had about 37.5 million inhabitants, making it the most populous country in east-central Europe. The population has been shrinking slightly for some years.

61348.q: What is the Hungarian name of the Great Hungarian Plain?
61348.e: “Alföld” means something like “lowland” and refers to the huge plain in the east and south of Hungary. It takes up about half of the country's area.
61348.m: In Hungarian, the Great Hungarian Plain is called the Alföld.

61349.q: Which river flows through the Great Hungarian Plain from north to south and is the most important tributary of the Danube in Hungary?
61349.e: The Tisza rises in the Carpathians of Ukraine and flows into the Danube in Serbia. It is the longest tributary of the Danube.
61349.m: The Tisza is the main river of the Hungarian Plain.

61350.q: What is the almost treeless steppe landscape of the Hungarian Plain called?
61350.e: The puszta is a wide, dry grassy steppe that formed partly naturally and partly through clearing and grazing. Typical sights are sweep wells and herdsmen with herds of cattle and horses.
61350.m: The puszta is Hungary's grassy steppe.

61351.q: Which national park, founded in 1973 as Hungary's first, protects a puszta landscape on the plain?
61351.e: Hortobágy National Park near Debrecen is the largest continuous steppe in Central Europe. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999.
61351.m: Hortobágy became Hungary's first national park in 1973.

61352.q: Which larger geological unit does the Great Hungarian Plain belong to?
61352.e: The Pannonian Basin is surrounded by the Carpathians, the Alps and the Dinarides. It is a sinking area filled with thick sediments.
61352.m: The Hungarian Plain lies in the Pannonian Basin.

61353.q: What covered the area of today's Hungarian Plain a few million years ago?
61353.e: In the Miocene, the Pannonian Sea, part of the Paratethys, lay here. Its deposits and later river sediments form the flat ground today.
61353.m: The plain was once covered by the Pannonian Sea.

61354.q: Which major project fundamentally changed the landscape of the plain from 1846?
a: The building of the Suez Canal
61354.e: Under István Széchenyi and the engineer Pál Vásárhelyi, the river was straightened and dyked. As a result, huge marshes became farmland, but wetlands were lost.
61354.m: In the 19th century the regulation of the Tisza turned marshes into farmland.

61355.q: Which towns on the Hungarian Plain are especially known for their paprika?
61355.e: The warm, sunny climate of the southern plain is good for growing paprika. Szeged and Kalocsa even have their own paprika museums.
61355.m: Szeged and Kalocsa are Hungary's paprika towns.

61356.q: Which hardy breed of cattle with long, curved horns is typical of the puszta?
61356.e: The grey Hungarian steppe cattle used to be driven in large herds as far as western Europe. Today they are kept as cultural heritage in national parks such as Hortobágy.
61356.m: Hungarian Grey cattle are a symbol of the puszta.

61357.q: What makes the Danube Delta push further out into the sea every year?
61357.e: The Danube carries large amounts of sand and mud, which are deposited at the mouth where the current slows down. This keeps creating new land.
61357.m: A delta grows through sediments that the river deposits at its mouth.

61358.q: In which country's territory does most of the Danube Delta lie?
61358.e: About four fifths of the delta lie in Romania, and the northern part in Ukraine. The delta is protected as a cross-border biosphere reserve.
61358.m: Most of the Danube Delta lies in Romania.

61359.q: Why was the Sulina branch of the Danube Delta straightened and deepened in the 19th century?
a: So that sea-going ships could sail from the sea into the Danube
So that the delta would dry out faster
So that fishing could be banned
So that Romania would get a new border
61359.e: From 1856 the European Commission of the Danube developed the Sulina branch into a shipping channel. This allowed ships to get from the Black Sea to the ports on the lower Danube.
61359.m: The Sulina branch is the shipping route in the Danube Delta.

61360.q: The Danube Delta is the second largest delta in Europe. Which delta is larger?
61360.e: The Volga Delta on the Caspian Sea is considerably larger than the Danube Delta. The Danube Delta, however, is the best-preserved large river delta in Europe.
61360.m: In Europe, only the Volga Delta is larger than the Danube Delta.

61361.q: Why is the Danube Delta especially important for birds?
a: It offers huge wetlands for breeding and resting
It is as warm as Africa in winter
It lies on the shortest route to America
There are no predators there at all
61361.e: Over 300 species of birds live and rest in the delta, including pelicans. It has been a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site since 1991.
61361.m: The Danube Delta is a paradise for birds and has been World Natural Heritage since 1991.

61362.q: Which plants form one of the largest continuous stands on Earth in the Danube Delta?
61362.e: Huge areas of reeds shape the delta and provide a habitat for many birds and fish. Reeds used to be harvested here on an industrial scale to make cellulose.
61362.m: The Danube Delta has huge reed beds.

61363.q: What have people in the villages of the Danube Delta traditionally lived on above all?
61363.e: Many villages in the delta can only be reached by boat. Fishing, reed harvesting and today tourism are the main sources of income; some fishermen are Lipovans, Old Believers from Russia.
61363.m: Many people in the Danube Delta live from fishing.

61364.q: Which international convention for the protection of wetlands lists the Danube Delta as a protected area?
61364.e: The Ramsar Convention of 1971 protects wetlands of international importance, especially as a habitat for water birds. The Danube Delta was added in 1991.
61364.m: The Ramsar Convention protects important wetlands such as the Danube Delta.

61365.q: Through which river does water from Switzerland reach the Danube Delta?
61365.e: The Inn rises in the Engadine, flows through Austria and joins the Danube at Passau. In this way, water from the Grisons eventually reaches the Black Sea.
61365.m: The Inn carries water from the Engadine all the way to the Black Sea.

61366.q: Which currency does the Republic of Moldova use (as of 2025)?
61366.e: The Moldovan leu was introduced in 1993. It should not be confused with the Romanian leu, which is used in Romania.
61366.m: In the Republic of Moldova you pay with the Moldovan leu.

61367.q: What is the breakaway, internationally unrecognised territory east of the Dniester called?
61367.e: Transnistria broke away in 1990, and in 1992 there was a short war. Russian troops have been stationed there ever since.
61367.m: Transnistria is a breakaway territory of the Republic of Moldova.

61368.q: Which autonomous region in southern Moldova is inhabited by an Orthodox Turkic people?
61368.e: The Gagauz speak a Turkic language close to Turkish but are Orthodox Christians. Gagauzia has had autonomous status since 1994.
61368.m: A Christian Turkic people lives in Gagauzia.

61369.q: Since a parliamentary decision in 2023, what is the official name of the official language of the Republic of Moldova?
61369.e: In 2023 parliament decided to replace the term “Moldovan language” with “Romanian language” in all laws. Linguistically, the two varieties are practically identical.
61369.m: Romanian is the official language of the Republic of Moldova.

61370.q: What is the village of Mileștii Mici in the Republic of Moldova known for?
a: The largest wine collection in the world
The largest coal power station in Europe
The longest bridge in eastern Europe
61370.e: About two million bottles are stored in underground cellars many kilometres long; Guinness World Records lists them as the largest wine collection. Winegrowing is an important part of Moldova's economy.
61370.m: Mileștii Mici has the largest wine collection in the world.

61371.q: As a landlocked country, how does the Republic of Moldova get access to sea shipping?
a: Through a short stretch of the Danube at Giurgiulești
Through a canal to the Black Sea
Through the port of Odesa as an exclave
Through its own strip of coast near Constanța
61371.e: Moldova has only about 500 metres of Danube bank, where the port of Giurgiulești lies. From there, sea-going ships can reach the Black Sea via the Danube.
61371.m: Giurgiulești is Moldova's only port with access to the sea.

61372.q: In which year did the Republic of Moldova declare its independence from the Soviet Union?
61372.e: The parliament in Chișinău declared independence on 27 August 1991, shortly before the Soviet Union collapsed. The day is now a national holiday.
61372.m: The Republic of Moldova has been independent since 1991.

61373.q: When did the Republic of Moldova, together with Ukraine, receive the status of an EU candidate country?
61373.e: The European Council granted both countries candidate status in June 2022. At the end of 2023 it was decided to open accession negotiations.
61373.m: Moldova has been an EU candidate since June 2022.

61374.q: What is the historic region between the Prut and the Dniester called, which forms most of today's Republic of Moldova?
61374.e: Bessarabia belonged to the Russian Empire from 1812, to Romania between the World Wars and then to the Soviet Union. The southern part is now in Ukraine.
61374.m: The core of the Republic of Moldova is historic Bessarabia.

61375.q: Which extensive area of marshes and forests shapes the south of Belarus?
61375.e: Polesia, along the River Pripyat, is one of the largest wetlands in Europe. It extends into Ukraine.
61375.m: Polesia is the great marshland in the south of Belarus.

61376.q: Which country received a particularly large share of the radioactive fallout after the Chernobyl disaster in 1986?
61376.e: Because of the wind direction, a very large part of the fallout came down over southern Belarus. Large areas of the Gomel region had to be evacuated.
61376.m: Belarus was hit especially hard by Chernobyl.

61377.q: Which river forms part of the border between Belarus and Poland and flows past Brest Fortress?
61377.e: For long stretches, the Western Bug forms the border between Poland on one side and Belarus and Ukraine on the other. At Brest the Mukhavets flows into it.
61377.m: The Bug is a border river between Belarus and Poland.

61378.q: Roughly how high is the highest point in Belarus, Dzyarzhynskaya Hara?
61378.e: Belarus is a very flat country; even its highest hill reaches only about 345 metres above sea level. By comparison, Bern lies at over 500 metres.
61378.m: Belarus is a flat country with no mountains over 400 metres.

61379.q: Which currency does Belarus use (as of 2025)?
61379.e: Belarus has its own currency, the Belarusian rouble. Despite close ties with Russia, the Russian rouble was never introduced.
61379.m: In Belarus you pay with the Belarusian rouble.

61380.q: Which mineral resource is especially important for the economy of Belarus and is mined near Salihorsk?
61380.e: Belarus is one of the largest potash producers in the world; the state company Belaruskali mines it near Salihorsk. Potash is mainly made into fertiliser.
61380.m: Belarus is a major producer of potash fertiliser.

61381.q: Which alliance did Belarus and Russia agree by treaty in 1999?
61381.e: The Union State is meant to link Belarus and Russia closely, both politically and economically. Many plans, such as a common currency, have not yet been carried out.
61381.m: Belarus and Russia have formed the Union State since 1999.

61382.q: Which lake is the largest in Belarus?
61382.e: Lake Narach in the north-west of the country covers about 80 square kilometres. Belarus has thousands of Ice Age lakes.
61382.m: Narach is the largest lake in Belarus.

61383.q: Which two castles in Belarus are UNESCO World Heritage Sites?
61383.e: Mir Castle combines Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque; Nesvizh was the residence of the noble Radziwiłł family. Both date from the time of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.
61383.m: Mir and Nesvizh castles are World Heritage in Belarus.

61384.q: What was the city of Kaliningrad called until 1946?
61384.e: Königsberg was the capital of East Prussia and came under Soviet administration in 1945. In 1946 it was renamed after the Soviet politician Mikhail Kalinin.
61384.m: Kaliningrad used to be called Königsberg.

61385.q: Which two countries does the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad border on land?
61385.e: Kaliningrad Oblast lies on the Baltic Sea between Poland and Lithuania. It has no land connection with the Russian mainland.

61386.q: Why is Kaliningrad considered an exclave and not an enclave?
a: It is not completely surrounded by a single foreign country
It does not belong to any country
It lies entirely on an island
61386.e: An enclave is completely surrounded by a single other country. Kaliningrad borders two countries and the sea, but it is cut off from the mother country and is therefore an exclave.
61386.m: An exclave is a part of a country that is cut off from the rest.

61387.q: Which raw material is mined on a large scale in the Kaliningrad region, where most of the world's reserves lie?
61387.e: In the open-cast mine near Yantarny, amber is extracted from Ice Age layers. The region holds about 90 per cent of the world's known amber deposits.
61387.m: Kaliningrad is the centre of amber mining worldwide.

61388.q: Which famous philosopher was born in Königsberg in 1724 and is buried there?
61388.e: Kant spent almost his whole life in Königsberg and taught at the university there. His grave is at the cathedral.
61388.m: Immanuel Kant lived and died in Königsberg.

61389.q: Which area of mathematics did Leonhard Euler found in 1736 with the problem of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg?
61389.e: The Basel mathematician Euler proved that it is impossible to cross all seven bridges exactly once and return to the start. This laid the foundation of graph theory.
61389.m: Leonhard Euler from Basel founded graph theory with the bridges of Königsberg.

61390.q: Why is Kaliningrad Oblast especially important for the Russian navy?
a: Its Baltic ports are ice-free even in winter
It lies directly on the open Atlantic
All Russian ships are built there
61390.e: Kaliningrad's ports, especially Baltiysk, stay ice-free in winter. The main base of the Russian Baltic Fleet is there.
61390.m: Kaliningrad is the Russian fleet's ice-free Baltic base.

61391.q: Which structure did Poland open through the Vistula Spit in 2022?
61391.e: The canal connects the Vistula Lagoon directly with the Baltic Sea. Ships heading for Elbląg no longer have to pass through the Russian strait at Baltiysk.
61391.m: Poland built a canal through the Vistula Spit.

61392.q: What is the narrow border strip between Poland and Lithuania called, which separates Kaliningrad from Belarus?
61392.e: The Suwałki Gap is only about 65 kilometres wide and connects the Baltic NATO states with Poland by land. That is why it is considered a strategically sensitive spot.
61392.m: The Suwałki Gap connects the Baltic states with Poland.

61393.q: Which especially fertile type of soil makes Ukraine the “breadbasket of Europe”?
61393.e: Black earth (chernozem) is rich in humus and formed under steppe grass. A large part of the world's black earth lies in Ukraine.
61393.m: Fertile black earth makes Ukraine a breadbasket.

61394.q: Of which farm product was Ukraine the world's largest exporter before 2022?
61394.e: Before the war, Ukraine supplied about half of the sunflower oil traded worldwide. Sunflowers grow well on the warm, dry steppe soils.
61394.m: Ukraine is the largest exporter of sunflower oil.

61395.q: What is the famine of 1932 and 1933 in Ukraine, caused by Soviet forced collectivisation, called?
61395.e: In the Holodomor, millions of people died because the state ruthlessly seized grain. Many countries recognise it as genocide.
61395.m: The Holodomor was the great famine in Ukraine in 1932 and 1933.

61396.q: Through which Black Sea port does Ukraine traditionally export most of its grain?
61396.e: Odesa and the neighbouring ports of Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi form Ukraine's most important export gateway. Most of the seaborne grain trade goes through them.
61396.m: Odesa is Ukraine's most important grain port.

61397.q: Which two parties brokered the grain deal in July 2022 for exporting Ukrainian grain across the Black Sea?
61397.e: The Black Sea Grain Initiative allowed safe shipments from Ukrainian ports until July 2023. Then Russia pulled out of the deal.
61397.m: The 2022 grain deal was brokered by the UN and Turkey.

61398.q: Roughly what share of Ukraine's land area is used for farming?
61398.e: Of about 60 million hectares of land, over 40 million hectares are farmland, most of it arable land. That is one of the highest shares in Europe.
61398.m: About two thirds of Ukraine is used for farming.

61399.q: Which river did Ukraine use from 2022 as an important alternative route for its grain exports?
61399.e: The Ukrainian Danube ports of Izmail and Reni were greatly expanded. From there the grain travels along the Danube to the Black Sea or on to Romania.
61399.m: From 2022 the Danube became an alternative route for Ukrainian grain.

61400.q: How are the colours of the Ukrainian flag often interpreted?
a: Blue sky over a yellow field of grain
Blue rivers and yellow sunflowers at night
Blue mountains and a yellow autumn forest
61400.e: A common interpretation sees the blue as the sky and the yellow as ripe wheat fields. It reflects the importance of farming for the country.
61400.m: The Ukrainian flag is often seen as sky over a wheat field.

61401.q: Which natural vegetation zone covers large parts of southern and eastern Ukraine?
61401.e: Ukraine's steppes are naturally grassland with hot summers and cold winters. Today they have almost all been turned into farmland.
61401.m: Most of Ukraine lies in the steppe zone.

61402.q: In EU usage, which of these countries no longer counts as part of the Western Balkans?
61402.e: Croatia has been an EU member since 2013 and is therefore no longer counted as part of the Western Balkans. The Western Balkans are Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia.
61402.m: As an EU member, Croatia no longer counts as part of the Western Balkans.

61403.q: With which neighbouring country did Macedonia sign the Prespa Agreement in 2018, which led to the name North Macedonia?
61403.e: Greece had rejected the name Macedonia because of its own region of the same name. Following the agreement, the country has been called North Macedonia since 2019.
61403.m: The Prespa Agreement with Greece brought the name North Macedonia.

61404.q: Roughly how long is the coast of Bosnia and Herzegovina at Neum?
61404.e: At Neum, Bosnia and Herzegovina reaches the Adriatic with a narrow strip. This corridor separates the Croatian area around Dubrovnik from the rest of Croatia.
61404.m: Bosnia and Herzegovina has only a very short coast at Neum.

61405.q: At which confluence does the Serbian capital, Belgrade, lie?
61405.e: Belgrade lies on a rocky ridge where the Sava flows into the Danube. Kalemegdan Fortress overlooks the confluence.
61405.m: Belgrade lies where the Sava flows into the Danube.

61406.q: Which bay on the Adriatic, with its old town, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979?
61406.e: The Bay of Kotor in Montenegro is surrounded by steep mountains and looks like a fjord. The fortified old town dates mostly from Venetian times.
61406.m: The Bay of Kotor is a World Heritage Site in Montenegro.

61407.q: Which famous bridge was destroyed in 1993 during the Bosnian War and rebuilt faithfully to the original in 2004?
61407.e: The Ottoman arched bridge over the Neretva dates from the 16th century. After being rebuilt, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
61407.m: The Old Bridge of Mostar was rebuilt after the war.

61408.q: Which initiative, launched by Germany in 2014, aims to bring the Western Balkan states closer to the EU?
61408.e: The Berlin Process promotes annual summits and projects on transport, energy and youth exchange. It is meant to strengthen regional cooperation and closer ties with the EU.
61408.m: Since 2014 the Berlin Process has brought the Western Balkans closer to the EU.

61409.q: What is the Swiss Army contingent called that has been deployed in Kosovo as part of KFOR since 1999?
61409.e: Swisscoy is a voluntary peace support mission of the Swiss Army. It supports the international security force KFOR.
61409.m: Since 1999 Swisscoy has supported peace in Kosovo.

61410.q: Which agreement ended the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995?
61410.e: The agreement negotiated in Dayton (USA) divided the country into two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska. It was signed in Paris in December 1995.
61410.m: The Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian War in 1995.

61411.q: What dams up many lakes in the south of the Finnish Lakeland?
a: End moraine ridges from the Ice Age
61411.e: The Salpausselkä formed when the edge of the ice stayed in one place for a long time after the Ice Age and deposited debris. These ridges dam up many lakes to the north.
61411.m: Ice Age end moraines dam up the Finnish Lakeland.

61412.q: The Punkaharju ridge in the Saimaa area is an esker. What is an esker?
a: The remains of an old volcano
A dune shaped by the wind
61412.e: An esker forms from sand and gravel that meltwater streams deposited in tunnels under the glacier. When the ice melts, a long, narrow ridge is left behind.
61412.m: An esker is a ridge of gravel that meltwater deposited under the ice.

61413.q: Why is the land in the Finnish Lakeland still slowly rising today?
a: Because of isostatic uplift after the Ice Age
Because of the collision of two continental plates
Because of rising magma under Finland
Because of the deposit of river sediments
61413.e: The weight of the thick ice sheet had pressed the Earth's crust down. Since the ice melted, it has been slowly springing back, which gradually changes lake shores and outflows.
61413.m: Finland is rising because the Earth's crust is springing back after the Ice Age.

61414.q: In which town of the Lakeland is a well-known opera festival held every summer in Olavinlinna Castle?
61414.e: The medieval castle of Olavinlinna stands on an island in Savonlinna. Opera festivals have been held there since 1912.
61414.m: In summer, opera is performed in Savonlinna's castle.

61415.q: Which canal connects the Saimaa lake system with the Gulf of Finland and runs partly through leased Russian territory?
61415.e: The Saimaa Canal opened in 1856 and runs from Lappeenranta to Vyborg. Its southern section has been in Russia since 1944; Finland has leased this part since 1963.
61415.m: The Saimaa Canal opens the Lakeland to the sea.

61416.q: On which large geological unit of ancient granite and gneiss does the Finnish Lakeland lie?
61416.e: The Baltic Shield is made of rocks more than a billion years old. Its hard, ground-down surface holds water in countless hollows.
61416.m: Finland lies on the ancient Baltic Shield.

61417.q: Into which large lake does the water of Finland's Saimaa drain via the River Vuoksi?
61417.e: The Vuoksi leaves Saimaa at Imatra and flows into Russia, into Lake Ladoga, the largest lake in Europe. From there the water reaches the Baltic Sea via the Neva.
61417.m: The Vuoksi carries Saimaa's water to Lake Ladoga.

61418.q: Roughly what share of Finland's area is covered by inland waters?
61418.e: Finland's lakes and rivers cover about 34,000 km² of a total area of about 338,000 km². That is roughly a tenth.
61418.m: About a tenth of Finland is covered by water.

61419.q: What is the Swedish right called that allows everyone to walk in nature, even on private land, and camp there briefly?
61419.e: The right of public access (allemansrätten, “everyman's right”) grants free access to nature but requires respect for property and the environment. It is mentioned in the Swedish constitution.
61419.m: The right of public access opens up nature to everyone in Sweden.

61420.q: Why do people in Sweden not pay with the euro, even though it is an EU member?
a: Voters rejected it in a referendum in 2003
Sweden does not meet the debt criteria
Sweden has only been in the EU since 2020
61420.e: Sweden joined the EU in 1995. In the 2003 referendum a majority rejected the euro, so the Swedish krona is still used.
61420.m: Sweden keeps the krona because voters rejected the euro in 2003.

61421.q: Which Swedish city has the largest port in the Nordic countries?
61421.e: Gothenburg lies where the Göta älv flows into the Kattegat and is ice-free. A large part of Scandinavia's foreign trade passes through its port.
61421.m: Gothenburg has the largest port in Scandinavia.

61422.q: Which Hanseatic town on the island of Gotland is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its town wall?
61422.e: In the Middle Ages, Visby was an important trading centre of the Hanseatic League. Its almost completely preserved town wall is about 3.4 km long.
61422.m: Visby on Gotland is an old Hanseatic town with a town wall.

61423.q: To which ice-free port is iron ore from Kiruna carried on the Ore Railway?
61423.e: The Ore Railway (Malmbanan) crosses the border to Narvik. Thanks to the North Atlantic Current, the port there does not freeze in winter, unlike Luleå on the Baltic.
61423.m: Swedish ore is shipped from Narvik, which is ice-free all year.

61424.q: Which Swedish coastal landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because the land there has risen by almost 300 m since the Ice Age?
61424.e: The High Coast has the highest known former shoreline in the world, at about 286 m. Together with the Finnish Kvarken Archipelago, it forms a shared World Heritage Site.
61424.m: On the High Coast you can see how much Scandinavia has risen.

61425.q: Until which year did the fertile region of Scania (Skåne) belong to Denmark?
61425.e: In the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658, Denmark had to give Scania to Sweden. Today the region is considered Sweden's breadbasket.

61426.q: Where does Sweden generate most of its hydroelectric power?
a: On the rivers of northern Sweden
On the lakes of southern Sweden
61426.e: Rivers such as the Lule älv and the Indalsälven flow from the Scandinavian Mountains to the Baltic Sea. Their drop is used in many power stations, and the electricity travels south over long power lines.
61426.m: Sweden's hydropower comes from the rivers of the north.

61427.q: What are the limestone pillars shaped by the sea on the coasts of Gotland and Fårö called?
61427.e: Waves and frost have worn away softer layers of rock and left the hard remains of an ancient reef standing. The pillars are often several metres high.
61427.m: Raukar are limestone pillars on the coast of Gotland.

61428.q: In geography, what else is the peninsula whose northern part forms Jutland called?
61428.e: The peninsula is named after the ancient people of the Cimbri. Its southern part belongs to Schleswig-Holstein, and the northern part is Danish Jutland.
61428.m: Jutland is the northern part of the Cimbrian Peninsula.

61429.q: Which arm of the sea cuts right through northern Jutland, so that the northernmost part is strictly speaking an island?
61429.e: Since a storm flood in the 19th century, the Limfjord has stretched from the North Sea to the Kattegat. The area north of it (Vendsyssel-Thy) is therefore separated from the mainland.
61429.m: The Limfjord separates the north of Jutland from the rest of the peninsula.

61430.q: Which two seas meet at the point of Grenen near Skagen?
61430.e: Grenen is the northernmost tip of Denmark. There you can see the waves of the Skagerrak and the Kattegat crash into each other.
61430.m: At Skagen, the Skagerrak and the Kattegat meet.

61431.q: Which town on the west coast of Jutland is considered the oldest town in Denmark?
61431.e: Ribe grew up in the early 8th century as a trading place of the Viking Age. The town lies on the edge of the Wadden Sea.
61431.m: Ribe is the oldest town in Denmark.

61432.q: Why was the port of Esbjerg on the west coast of Jutland founded in 1868?
a: Denmark had lost Schleswig, and with it its western port, in 1864
A ferry to Norway was planned
Oil had been discovered off the coast
The old port of Ribe had burned down
61432.e: After the Second Schleswig War of 1864, Denmark lacked a large North Sea port. Esbjerg was therefore newly built and is today a centre of the offshore wind industry.
61432.m: Esbjerg was founded as a new North Sea port after Schleswig was lost.

61433.q: How did North Schleswig return to Denmark in 1920?
61433.e: After the First World War, the Treaty of Versailles provided for referendums in Schleswig. The northern part voted mostly for Denmark, which created today's border.
61433.m: In 1920 North Schleswig voted in a referendum to join Denmark.

61434.q: Which city is the largest in Jutland and the second largest in Denmark?
61434.e: Aarhus lies on the east coast of Jutland and has a large university and an important port. Odense, on the other hand, is on the island of Funen.
61434.m: Aarhus is Denmark’s second largest city.

61435.q: How were the sandy soils in western Jutland mainly formed?
a: By outwash plains from Ice Age meltwater
By coral reefs from the Cretaceous period
61435.e: Meltwater rivers in front of the ice margin laid down large areas of sand and gravel in the west. Heathland used to spread across these nutrient-poor soils.
61435.m: Western Jutland consists of Ice Age outwash plains.

61436.q: Which landscape in County Clare is known for its bare limestone pavements?
61436.e: In the Burren the limestone lies exposed with almost no soil, and rainwater has dissolved cracks and grooves in it. Even so, Arctic, Alpine and Mediterranean plants grow side by side there.
61436.m: The Burren is a karst landscape in the west of Ireland.

61437.q: What is Ireland’s strong economic boom of the 1990s often called?
61437.e: Low corporate taxes, a well-trained workforce and EU funding attracted many international companies. The term is based on the Asian Tiger economies.
61437.m: Ireland’s boom of the 1990s is called the Celtic Tiger.

61438.q: Which type of wetland covers large parts of central and western Ireland and was dug for fuel for a long time?
61438.e: Peat has built up in Ireland’s raised bogs over thousands of years. It was cut and burned; today many bogs are being restored to protect the climate.
61438.m: Irish bogs supply peat and store a lot of carbon.

61439.q: What are the hexagonal columns of the Giant’s Causeway in the north of the island of Ireland made of?
61439.e: Around 60 million years ago, basalt lava cooled slowly there and contracted. This created the regular columns.
61439.m: The Giant’s Causeway is made of basalt columns.

61440.q: Which Ice Age landform, whose name comes from Irish, shapes large parts of northern and central Ireland?
61440.e: Drumlins are long, streamlined hills of moraine material that formed beneath the glacier. The word comes from the Irish “droim” meaning back or ridge.
61440.m: Drumlins are hills shaped by ice.

61441.q: According to the Irish constitution, which language is the country’s first official language?
61441.e: The 1937 constitution names Irish as the national language and first official language, with English as the second. In everyday life, however, most people speak English.
61441.m: Irish is Ireland’s first official language.

61442.q: Which 1998 agreement largely ended the conflict in Northern Ireland?
61442.e: The Good Friday Agreement created a shared government of both communities in Northern Ireland. That is why, after Brexit, people wanted to avoid checks at the border on the island of Ireland.
61442.m: The Good Friday Agreement brought peace to Northern Ireland in 1998.

61443.q: What happens every year at the winter solstice in the passage tomb of Newgrange?
a: The morning sun lights up the inner chamber
A fire is lit inside it
61443.e: The tomb in the Boyne Valley, about 5000 years old, has a roof box above the entrance. Only around 21 December does sunlight shine down the passage into the chamber.
61443.m: At Newgrange the winter sunlight reaches the burial chamber.

61444.q: What was the standard rate of corporation tax with which Ireland attracted international companies for decades?
61444.e: The 12.5% rate was among the lowest in Europe. Since 2024, a minimum rate of 15% has applied to very large international companies because of an OECD agreement.
61444.m: Ireland attracted firms for a long time with 12.5% corporation tax.

61445.q: At 1345 m, which mountain is the highest in the United Kingdom?
61445.e: Ben Nevis lies near Fort William in the western Highlands. It is the remains of an ancient volcano.
61445.m: Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in Great Britain.

61446.q: Along which major fault does Loch Ness lie?
61446.e: The Great Glen Fault runs diagonally across Scotland from Inverness to Fort William. Several long, deep lochs lie along this fault zone.
61446.m: Loch Ness lies in the Great Glen fault zone.

61447.q: What was the result of the 2014 Scottish independence referendum?
a: About 55% voted to stay in the United Kingdom
61447.e: On 18 September 2014, 55.3% voted No to independence. Scotland therefore remained part of the United Kingdom.

61448.q: With which law did Scotland and England join to form the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1707?
61448.e: The Acts of Union united the parliaments of both countries in London. Only in 1999 did Scotland once again get its own parliament in Edinburgh.
61448.m: The Act of Union of 1707 united Scotland and England.

61449.q: What are the evictions of small farmers from the Scottish Highlands in the 18th and 19th centuries called?
61449.e: Landowners drove out tenants so they could use the land for profitable sheep farming. Many of those affected emigrated to Canada, Australia or the USA.
61449.m: The Highland Clearances emptied the Scottish Highlands.

61450.q: Which well-preserved Stone Age village lies on the Orkney Islands?
61450.e: Skara Brae was lived in around 3100 BC. In 1850 a storm uncovered the houses buried under sand, complete with stone furniture.
61450.m: Skara Brae is a Stone Age village on Orkney.

61451.q: Which realm did the Orkney and Shetland Islands belong to before they were pledged to Scotland in 1468/69?
61451.e: King Christian I pledged the islands as a dowry for his daughter. The pledge was never redeemed, and the Nordic influence can still be seen today.
61451.m: Orkney and Shetland used to be Nordic.

61452.q: In Scotland, what does a “firth”, as in the Firth of Forth, mean?
a: A wide sea inlet or estuary
A mountain lake in the Highlands
61452.e: A firth is a wide arm of the sea, often the funnel-shaped mouth of a river. The capital, Edinburgh, lies on the Firth of Forth.
61452.m: In Scotland a firth is a wide sea inlet.

61453.q: According to the 2021 census, what share of the population of Wales could speak Welsh?
61453.e: The 2021 census found that 17.8% of people aged three and over spoke Welsh. The Welsh Government aims to reach one million speakers by 2050.
61453.m: Just under a fifth of people in Wales speak Welsh.

61454.q: Which raw material shaped the valleys of South Wales, such as the Rhondda Valley, in the 19th century?
61454.e: South Wales was one of the most important coalfields in the world. As a result, Cardiff became one of the largest coal ports.
61454.m: The valleys of South Wales lived from coal mining.

61455.q: Which landscape in North Wales became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 because of the stone that used to be quarried there?
61455.e: In the 19th century North Wales supplied roofing slate to the whole world. The quarries, railways and villages of this industry are now World Heritage.
61455.m: North Wales was a world centre of slate quarrying.

61456.q: Since when has Cardiff officially been the capital of Wales?
61456.e: Cardiff was only officially declared the capital in 1955. Before that, Wales had no recognised capital.
61456.m: Cardiff has been the capital of Wales since 1955.

61457.q: Which national park in south-west Wales is protected mainly because of its coast?
61457.e: The national park was founded in 1952 and consists almost entirely of coastal landscape. A coast path about 300 km long runs through it.
61457.m: The Pembrokeshire Coast National Park protects a coastline.

61458.q: What is the 8th-century earthwork called that roughly follows the border between England and Wales?
61458.e: King Offa of Mercia had the earthwork built against the Welsh kingdoms. Today a long footpath follows it.
61458.m: Offa’s Dyke marks the old border with Wales.

61459.q: Which English king had Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech castles built in North Wales in the 13th century?
61459.e: After conquering Wales in 1283, Edward I secured his rule with a ring of mighty castles. Several of them are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
61459.m: Edward I built the great castles in North Wales.

61460.q: Which river, the longest in Great Britain, rises in the mountains of Wales?
61460.e: The Severn rises on Plynlimon and flows through Wales and England into the Bristol Channel. It is about 350 km long.
61460.m: The Severn is Great Britain’s longest river.

61461.q: What cooperation did the governments in exile of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg agree on in London in 1944?
61461.e: The London Customs Convention came into force in 1948 and created the Benelux customs union. It is seen as a model for later European integration.
61461.m: The Benelux countries founded a customs union after the Second World War.

61462.q: How many regions does the federal state of Belgium have?
61462.e: Belgium is divided into the regions of Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital. In addition, there are three language communities.

61463.q: Roughly what share of the area of the Netherlands lies below sea level?
61463.e: About 26% of the country lies below mean sea level. These areas are protected by dykes, dunes and pumping stations.
61463.m: A quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level.

61464.q: What is the urban area with Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht called?
61464.e: The Randstad forms a ring of cities around a green, farmed heart. Almost half of the Dutch population lives there.
61464.m: The Randstad is the urban centre of the Netherlands.

61465.q: Where is Belgium’s highest point, the Signal de Botrange?
61465.e: The Signal de Botrange is 694 m high and lies on the raised bog plateau of the High Fens. It is part of the foothills of the Ardennes.
61465.m: Belgium’s highest point lies in the High Fens.

61466.q: Which languages are official languages in Belgium?
61466.e: A legal language border separates Dutch-speaking Flanders from French-speaking Wallonia. In the east there is also a small German-speaking community.

61467.q: Via which river is the port of Antwerp connected to the North Sea, with its mouth in the Netherlands?
61467.e: The Western Scheldt lies on Dutch territory. Deepening it for large ships therefore had to be settled in treaties between the two countries.
61467.m: Antwerp reaches the sea via the Scheldt.

61468.q: Why was the Eastern Scheldt not fully dammed but protected by a storm surge barrier with movable gates?
a: To keep the tides and the saltwater habitat
Because a dam would have been too expensive
Because the ground could not support a dam
To save ships from passing through
61468.e: After protests from fishermen and conservationists, an open barrier was chosen in 1976. The gates only close during storm surges; otherwise the sea flows freely in and out.
61468.m: The Eastern Scheldt barrier only closes during storm surges.

61469.q: Which sandy landscape in north-east Belgium was a coalfield in the 20th century?
61469.e: In the Kempen (Campine) in the province of Limburg, coal was mined at great depth from 1917. The last mine closed in 1992.
61469.m: The Kempen in north-east Belgium was a coalfield.

61470.q: In which area is Luxembourg the largest financial centre in Europe?
61470.e: Funds with assets of several thousand billion euros are managed in Luxembourg. After the USA, it is the second largest fund centre in the world.
61470.m: Luxembourg is Europe’s largest fund centre.

61471.q: Which European bank has its headquarters in Luxembourg?
a: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
61471.e: The European Investment Bank (EIB) grants long-term loans for projects in the interest of the EU. The ECB is based in Frankfurt, the BIS in Basel.
61471.m: The European Investment Bank is based in Luxembourg.

61472.q: Why can funds authorised in Luxembourg be sold throughout the EU?
a: Thanks to an EU passport for authorised funds
Because Luxembourg is the capital of the EU
Because Luxembourg has no fund supervision
Because all EU funds must be based in Luxembourg
61472.e: Under the EU rules for funds (UCITS), a fund authorised in one EU country may be sold in all other member states. The fund centre of Luxembourg benefits greatly from this.
61472.m: An EU passport allows funds to be sold throughout the EU.

61473.q: Which type of bond was first issued by the European Investment Bank in 2007 and listed in Luxembourg?
61473.e: The EIB’s “Climate Awareness Bond” is considered the world’s first green bond. The Luxembourg Stock Exchange now runs its own platform for sustainable bonds.
61473.m: The first green bond was listed in Luxembourg.

61474.q: From 2015, Luxembourg automatically exchanged account information with other EU countries. What was largely given up as a result?
a: Banking secrecy towards foreign tax authorities
61474.e: Under international pressure, Luxembourg took part in the automatic exchange of information. Switzerland also adopted this standard from 2017.
61474.m: With the automatic exchange of information, banking secrecy ended for foreign tax authorities.

61475.q: Where do almost half of the people working in Luxembourg come from?
a: From neighbouring countries as cross-border commuters
61475.e: Every day over 200,000 people commute to Luxembourg from France, Belgium and Germany. This makes GDP per head particularly high, because the commuters work there but are not counted as residents.
61475.m: Many workers in Luxembourg are cross-border commuters.

61476.q: With which country did Luxembourg form an economic and currency union from 1921?
61476.e: The Belgium-Luxembourg Economic Union firmly linked the two currencies. The Belgian franc was also valid in Luxembourg until the euro arrived in 2002.
61476.m: From 1921 Luxembourg was closely linked economically with Belgium.

61477.q: Which institution of the euro countries, which gives loans to countries in financial difficulty, is based in Luxembourg?
61477.e: The ESM was founded in 2012 as the permanent rescue fund of the eurozone. It grants loans in return for reforms.
61477.m: The euro rescue fund ESM is based in Luxembourg.

61478.q: Which tax do most residents of Monaco not pay?
61478.e: Monaco does not charge income tax on individuals. French citizens are an exception because of an agreement from 1963.
61478.m: In Monaco most people pay no income tax.

61479.q: How has Monaco increased its area in recent decades?
a: By reclaiming land from the sea
61479.e: The district of Fontvieille was built on land reclaimed from the sea from the 1970s. Most recently, the Mareterra district was added.
61479.m: Monaco gains new land from the sea.

61480.q: Who may vote for Monaco’s parliament, the National Council?
a: Only members of the princely family
61480.e: The Conseil national has 24 members and is elected every five years. Because only about a quarter of residents are Monégasques, the majority cannot vote.
61480.m: In Monaco only Monégasques elect the parliament.

61481.q: Why did Monaco rely on the Monte Carlo Casino in the 19th century?
a: It needed new income after losing territory
61481.e: Menton and Roquebrune broke away in 1848 and were handed over to France in 1861. Monaco lost about four fifths of its territory and much tax income. Prince Charles III therefore relied on a casino and tourism.
61481.m: After losing Menton and Roquebrune, Monaco relied on the casino.

61482.q: Who is not allowed to enter the gaming rooms of the Monte Carlo Casino as a player?
61482.e: Prince Charles III banned his own citizens from gambling in the casino. The casino was meant to bring in money from visitors, not to ruin the locals.
61482.m: Monégasques may not gamble in their own casino.

61483.q: With which country does Monaco form a customs union?
61483.e: Because of the customs union, there are no customs checks at the border with France. Through France, Monaco is also linked to the EU customs area.
61483.m: Monaco and France form a customs union.

61484.q: Roughly what share of Monaco’s residents hold Monégasque citizenship?
61484.e: In the 2016 census, about 9300 of just over 37,000 residents were Monégasques. The largest of the other groups are French and Italian.
61484.m: Only about a quarter of people in Monaco are Monégasques.

61485.q: What is the district on the rock where the Prince’s Palace stands called?
61485.e: Monaco-Ville sits on a rocky headland above the sea and is called “Le Rocher”. The cathedral and the town hall also stand there.
61485.m: The Prince’s Palace stands in Monaco-Ville on the rock.

61486.q: What is special about the capital Andorra la Vella?
a: It is the highest capital in Europe
It is the oldest capital in Europe
It is the southernmost capital in Europe
It is the smallest capital in Europe
61486.e: Andorra la Vella lies at about 1000 m above sea level in a Pyrenean valley. No other capital in Europe is higher.
61486.m: Andorra la Vella is Europe’s highest capital.

61487.q: Who are the two heads of state (co-princes) of Andorra today?
a: The Bishop of Urgell and the President of France
The King of Spain and the Pope
The President of France and the King of Spain
Two presidents elected by the people
61487.e: The joint rule goes back to a treaty from 1278. The rights of the Count of Foix later passed to the French kings and today to the French president.
61487.m: Andorra has two co-princes: a bishop and the President of France.

61488.q: What does Andorra’s economy mainly live on?
a: Tourism, such as winter sports and shopping
61488.e: Andorra attracts millions of visitors who ski in the Pyrenees or shop cheaply because of low taxes. The Madriu-Perafita-Claror valley is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

61489.q: What is the parliament of Andorra called?
61489.e: The Consell General has 28 members. Half are elected nationwide and the other half in the parishes.
61489.m: Andorra’s parliament is called the Consell General.

61490.q: Which language is Andorra’s only official language?
61490.e: Although Andorra lies between Spain and France, Catalan is the only official language. Spanish and French are also widely spoken in daily life.
61490.m: Catalan is the official language of Andorra.

61491.q: Into which large Spanish river does the water of the Gran Valira from Andorra finally flow?
61491.e: The Gran Valira flows into the Segre near La Seu d’Urgell. The Segre continues into the Ebro and so into the Mediterranean.
61491.m: Andorra’s water flows via the Segre into the Ebro.

61492.q: Which tax did Andorra only introduce for individuals in 2015?
61492.e: For a long time Andorra was seen as a country with almost no direct taxes. Under pressure from the EU, it introduced an income tax in 2015 with a top rate of 10%.
61492.m: Andorra has only had an income tax since 2015.

61493.q: What arrangement has Andorra had with the European Community since 1991?
a: A customs union for industrial goods
61493.e: There are no customs duties on industrial goods between Andorra and the EU. However, Andorra is neither an EU member nor part of the Schengen Area.
61493.m: Andorra forms a customs union with the EU for industrial goods.

61494.q: Roughly how large is the area of San Marino?
61494.e: At about 61 km², San Marino is the fifth smallest country in the world. Only Vatican City, Monaco, Nauru and Tuvalu are smaller.
61494.m: San Marino covers about 61 square kilometres.

61495.q: What are the nine municipalities that San Marino is divided into called?
61495.e: San Marino is divided into nine castelli, including the capital, the City of San Marino. Each castello has its own council.
61495.m: San Marino consists of nine castelli.

61496.q: According to its own tradition, what is San Marino known for?
a: It is considered the oldest surviving republic in the world
It is the smallest country in the world
It has no government of its own
It is a member of the EU
61496.e: According to tradition, San Marino was founded in the year 301. Vatican City and Monaco, for example, are smaller, and it does not belong to the EU.
61496.m: San Marino is considered the oldest republic in the world.

61497.q: Which offer is San Marino said to have turned down from Napoleon in 1797?
a: A seaport of its own as a gift
61497.e: Napoleon offered to expand the country’s territory. San Marino declined so as not to put its independence and neutrality at risk.
61497.m: San Marino turned down Napoleon’s offer of more land.

61498.q: How long is the term of office of San Marino’s two Captains Regent?
61498.e: The regents take office on 1 April and 1 October. The short term is meant to stop anyone from gathering too much power, similar to the Swiss Federal Presidency that changes every year.
61498.m: San Marino’s regents change every six months.

61499.q: Which US president became an honorary citizen of San Marino in 1861?
61499.e: San Marino offered Lincoln honorary citizenship. He thanked them in a letter and praised the small republic.
61499.m: Abraham Lincoln was an honorary citizen of San Marino.

61500.q: What can be seen from far away on Monte Titano and is also shown on San Marino’s coat of arms?
61500.e: The three towers Guaita, Cesta and Montale stand on the peaks of Monte Titano. They are the country’s landmark and appear on its flag and coat of arms.
61500.m: Three towers are San Marino’s landmark.

61501.q: How has San Marino traditionally earned money from collectors around the world?
61501.e: San Marino issues its own stamps and its own euro coins in small numbers. Many of them are not used in everyday life but collected.
61501.m: Stamps and coins from San Marino are popular with collectors.

61502.q: Which three inhabited islands make up the country of Malta?
61502.e: Gozo is the second largest and Comino the smallest inhabited island. Lampedusa, Linosa and Pantelleria belong to Italy.
61502.m: Malta consists of Malta, Gozo and Comino.

61503.q: Which order of knights founded the capital Valletta in 1566?
61503.e: Grand Master Jean de la Valette gave the city its name. The Knights of St John ruled Malta from 1530 to 1798.
61503.m: The Knights of St John founded Valletta.

61504.q: Against whom did the knights on Malta defend themselves in the Great Siege of 1565?
61504.e: A large Ottoman fleet besieged the island for months without success. The victory made Malta famous throughout Europe.
61504.m: Malta withstood the Ottoman siege in 1565.

61505.q: How does Malta meet a large part of its drinking water needs?
61505.e: Malta has no rivers and hardly any rain in summer. Reverse osmosis plants therefore supply a large part of the tap water.
61505.m: Malta gets drinking water from the sea.

61506.q: Which award did the whole island of Malta receive in 1942 for its resistance in the Second World War?
61506.e: King George VI awarded the George Cross to the people, who endured heavy air raids. The cross appears on Malta’s flag today.
61506.m: The George Cross on Malta’s flag recalls the Second World War.

61507.q: What is the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum on Malta?
a: A tunnel of the Knights of St John
61507.e: The chambers cut into the rock were made around 4000 BC. The remains of about 7000 people were found inside.
61507.m: The Hypogeum is a Stone Age burial site cut into the rock.

61508.q: Since which year have people in Malta paid with the euro?
61508.e: On 1 January 2008, Malta replaced the Maltese lira with the euro. Cyprus switched at the same time as Malta.
61508.m: Malta has had the euro since 2008.

61509.q: Who drove the Knights of St John out of Malta in 1798?
61509.e: On his way to Egypt, Napoleon captured the island almost without a fight. By 1800 the British had taken control.
61509.m: Napoleon ended the rule of the Knights of St John on Malta in 1798.

61510.q: After Malta’s independence in 1964, who was still head of state at first?
a: The Grand Master of the Knights of St John
61510.e: After 1964 Malta remained a monarchy with Elizabeth II as queen. Only in 1974 did the country become a republic with its own president.
61510.m: Malta has been a republic since 1974.

61511.q: In the geography of Spain, what is the “Meseta”?
a: The central plateau of the Iberian Peninsula
The coastal plain on the Mediterranean
The mountain range on the border with France
61511.e: The Meseta is the vast high plateau in the interior of Spain. The name means something like “little table” and refers to its flat, raised shape.
61511.m: The Meseta is the high plateau at the heart of Spain.

61512.q: Which river drains most of the northern Meseta?
61512.e: The Douro (Duero in Spanish) collects the water of the northern plateau and flows into the Atlantic at Porto.
